questions.q: How do you limit a result set to 10 rows in idiomatic Snowflake SQL?
options: SELECT TOP 10 ... (identical placement to T-SQL, with no LIMIT support at all)
SELECT ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT 10 (LIMIT goes at the end of the query)
Snowflake cannot limit result sets
SELECT ... WHERE ROWCOUNT = 10
questions.explain: Snowflake places LIMIT at the end of the query, after ORDER BY. It also accepts TOP for compatibility, but LIMIT is the idiomatic form.

questions.q: What operator does Snowflake use for string concatenation?
options: || (double pipe)
& (ampersand)
CONCAT_STR()
+ (plus sign, same as T-SQL)
questions.explain: Snowflake reserves + for arithmetic only; string concatenation uses ||  (a CONCAT() function also exists, but || is the standard idiom).

questions.q: What is Snowflake's IFF() function equivalent to in T-SQL?
options: There is no T-SQL equivalent
IIF() — same single-condition conditional logic, different spelling
CASE WHEN, with completely different syntax
MERGE
questions.explain: IFF(condition, true_result, false_result) behaves exactly like T-SQL's IIF() — just spelled with one fewer letter.

questions.q: What does Snowflake's QUALIFY clause let you do that has no direct T-SQL equivalent?
options: Filter rows before any WHERE clause is applied
Join two tables without specifying a join condition
Filter directly on a window function's result (like ROW_NUMBER) without needing a wrapping CTE
Run a query without selecting a warehouse
questions.explain: In T-SQL, filtering on a window function forces a CTE or subquery because WHERE can't see window function results. QUALIFY filters on the window function directly, in the same query.

questions.q: How does Snowflake handle unquoted identifiers by default?
options: It rejects any identifier that isn't fully uppercase
Case-sensitively, always exactly as typed
Case-insensitively — they're folded to uppercase internally, same behavior covered in Lesson 3
Identically to how T-SQL's default collation always behaves
questions.explain: Unquoted identifiers are case-insensitive in Snowflake and folded to uppercase — a behavior you shouldn't assume matches whatever collation a given T-SQL instance happens to use.
